newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE VICTORY SWEEPS ASIDE ALL DOUBTS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE VICTORY SWEEPS ASIDE ALL DOUBTS.

text.p: Any doubts about Jacques Villeneuve's talent or his potential to become world champion were swept aside by his victory in Sunday's Portuguese Grand Prix.
The Canadian's drive from fourth at the end of the first lap to triumph kept alive his hopes of becoming the first man to win the Indycar and Formula One world titles in successive seasons.

Briton Damon Hill, his Williams team mate and hot favourite for the drivers' title with a nine point lead, admitted: "What Jacques did was pretty fantastic. It is difficult to overtake on this circuit, but to get through the traffic here and move from fourth to the front is something special."

Double world champion Michael Schumacher of Ferrari, who was third and ahead of Villeneuve over the opening laps, said he had been stunned when he saw the French-Canadian pass him on the outside of the final parabolica corner, a move not previously seen at Estoril.
"I was very surprised," he said. "I did not know where he was. Then suddenly he was alongside me and I could not do much to stop him getting by. It was a very brave move."
Villeneuve said he had talked to his team's engineers about attempting to pass on the outside of that corner and had been warned that it was too risky.
"I was sure we could do it," he said. "They said they would come and pick me out of the guard rail if I tried it.

"Actually, if we hadn't hit any traffic I don't think it would have been possible. But I had nothing to lose. Either I beat Damon or I lost the championship right there anyway. So, it was worth it to take a big risk."

Villeneuve's startling passing move on Schumacher was the highlight of his excellent drive and will give him a psychological boost as he begins the preparations for the final showdown for the title in Suzuka, Japan on October 13.

Hill, with a comfortable lead needs only one point or the equivalent of a sixth-place finish to become champion. Hill has 87 points and Villeneuve 78, but if Villeneuve won and Hill finished sixth, bringing them level on 88, the Briton would take the title because he has won more races this season than Villeneuve.
If Hill fails to finish in Japan, Villeneuve still must win the race to become champion.
Although Hill has not won any of his last four races, he knows that Villeneuve not only has to beat him, but also resist the mounting challenges from Ferrari, Benetton and McLaren at Suzuka.

Schumacher, in his Ferrari, will be a strong challenger again in Japan and a truly titanic battle for victory between the German and the Canadian may not only decide the outcome of this year's drivers' championship -- probably in Hill's favour -- but also provide a taste of what lies ahead next season.

Hill's future, however, remains unknown after his failure to take the title with an emphatic performance. He now seems likely to sign for Jordan later this week, or next, after his testing duties with the Williams team are over.
Both Hill and Villeneuve are expected to return to Estoril on Tuesday for four days' work which will partly concentrate on Suzuka and partly on 1997, when Hill will no longer be with the team.

He made it clear at the weekend that he had little chance to even think about any discussions with other teams because he was concentrating on the race. But in the next 10 days, he will almost certainly turn his mind to other plans.

On Sunday, he said that retirement was certainly not one of his options. "I hope to be here in Formula One again next year," he said. "I am not thinking about retiring. After all the money is not as good in retirement, is it?"
